text: A text is hateful if it attacks, demeans, dehumanises, or calls for harm against a person or group because of a protected characteristic such as race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, disability, or national origin. Offensive or rude language alone, without a protected-group target, is not hate speech.

label: race
text: The text targets people because of their race, skin colour, or ethnicity, e.g. Black, Asian, Hispanic, Arab, or white people as a group.

label: religion
text: The text targets people because of their religion or belief, e.g. Muslims, Jews, Christians, Hindus.

label: gender
text: The text targets people because of their gender, including misogyny and attacks on trans people.

label: sexual_orientation
text: The text targets people because of their sexual orientation, e.g. gay, lesbian, bisexual people.

label: disability
text: The text targets people because of a physical or mental disability.

label: national_origin
text: The text targets people because of their nationality, immigration or refugee status.

label: other
text: The text targets a protected group not listed above, for example people singled out by age, veteran or military status, caste, socioeconomic class or poverty, homelessness, immigration detention status, body size or physical appearance, or occupation. Use this label only when a protected group is clearly identified and none of the specific labels apply.

label: explicit
text: Openly hateful; slurs or direct attacks.

label: incitement
text: Calls for or glorifies violence or hateful action against the group.

label: inferiority
text: Claims the group is inferior, subhuman, or of less worth.

label: irony
text: Uses sarcasm, jokes, or irony to demean the group.

label: stereotyping
text: Attributes negative characteristics to the whole group, incl. hateful misinformation.

label: threatening
text: Threatens or intimidates the group or its members.

label: grievance
text: Frames the in-group as victims of the targeted group (e.g. white grievance).

label: low
text: Hateful, but comparatively mild in intensity: insults, slurs, or derogatory remarks that demean a protected group without extreme hostility.

label: medium
text: Strongly hostile: heavy or repeated slurs and clearly degrading language directed at a protected group.

label: high
text: Extremely hostile: the most intense hate, including incitement, threats, or calls for violence, as well as the most severe degradation.

label: propaganda
text: The text distributes propaganda material, or uses symbols, slogans, or greetings of an organisation ruled unconstitutional in Germany, particularly content promoting a former National Socialist organisation. Examples include banned party slogans and coded references to them. German Criminal Code sections 86 and 86a.

label: incitement_public_peace
text: The text publicly calls for criminal offences, threatens serious crimes, incites hatred or violence against a national, racial, religious or ethnic group, glorifies violence, or approves of or rewards serious crimes. Includes Volksverhetzung, the German provision most directly concerned with hate speech. A call must be concrete: the act, and ideally the time, place or victim, should be identifiable. German Criminal Code sections 111, 126, 130, 131, 140.

label: insult_defamation
text: The text insults a person or a legally recognised collective, spreads a damaging claim that is not demonstrably true, or abuses a religious or ideological community over its beliefs. Statements about public figures are judged more permissively than statements about private individuals. German Criminal Code sections 166, 185, 186.

Quoting or reporting a slur - in news, testimony, counter-speech, or condemnation - is not itself hate speech. The test is whether the author endorses the attack, not whether a slur appears in the text.
A slur used by a member of the targeted group about their own group (reclaimed or in-group use) is generally not hate speech. Context and speaker matter more than the presence of the word.
Counter-speech that names or describes hate in order to oppose, challenge, or condemn it is not hate speech, even when it repeats the hateful content it argues against.
Sarcasm, irony, or jokes that demean a protected group ARE hate speech. Humorous framing does not neutralise an attack on a group based on a protected characteristic.

Criticism of a religion's ideas, doctrines, or practices is not hate speech. Attacks on, or dehumanisation of, its believers as people because of their faith IS hate speech. The target - ideas vs people - is the distinction.
Profanity, insults, or aggression without a protected-characteristic target is not hate speech. "You idiot" or generic rudeness is offensive but not hate unless it attacks a protected group.

An attack on an individual for personal reasons is not hate speech. It becomes hate speech when the person is attacked as a representative of a protected group, or the attack generalises to the whole group.
Hate speech need not contain slurs. Coded language, dog whistles, stereotypes stated as fact, and implied dehumanisation can be hate speech even when no explicit slur appears.
Calls for violence, exclusion, deportation, or harm against a protected group, and statements that such harm is deserved or desirable, are hate speech of the most severe kind.
Hate speech can target majority or powerful groups, not only minorities. The test is an attack based on a protected characteristic, regardless of the group's social status.
Statements that explicitly reject or negate hate ("I don't think women are inferior") are not hate speech. Attend to negation - surface keywords alone can flip the meaning.

Eine Aufforderung zu einer Straftat ist nur dann strafrechtlich relevant, wenn sie konkret ist. Tatzeit, Ort oder Opfer sollten erkennbar sein. Je konkreter die Formulierung, desto eher ist der Kommentar strafbar. Vage Wut oder allgemeine Ablehnung reicht nicht.

Aussagen gegen Personen des oeffentlichen Lebens werden milder beurteilt als Aussagen gegen Privatpersonen. Politikerinnen und Politiker muessen scharfe Kritik und auch Beschimpfungen eher hinnehmen. Dieselbe Beleidigung kann gegenueber einer Privatperson strafbar und gegenueber einer oeffentlichen Person straffrei sein.

Nicht jede Beschimpfung ist eine strafbare Beleidigung. Ausdruecke wie Depp oder Arschloch sind nicht immer strafrechtlich relevant. Herabwuerdigende sexualisierte Schimpfwoerter sind es in der Regel schon. Entscheidend ist, ob ein Werturteil mit dem Ziel der Herabwuerdigung abgegeben wird.

Volksverhetzung liegt vor, wenn zu Hass oder Gewalt gegen Personen wegen ihrer Zugehoerigkeit zu einer nationalen, rassischen, religioesen oder ethnischen Gruppe aufgerufen wird, oder wenn die Menschenwuerde dieser Gruppen durch Beschimpfung oder Verleumdung angegriffen wird. Dieser Paragraf betrifft Hassrede am unmittelbarsten.

Parolen, Gruszformeln und Kennzeichen verbotener oder verfassungswidriger Organisationen sind strafrechtlich relevant, insbesondere Bezuege auf nationalsozialistische Organisationen. Der Kontext entscheidet: aehnlich klingende Parolen ohne historischen Bezug sind es nicht. Im Zweifel ist zu pruefen, ob sich der Ausdruck auf ein konkretes Ereignis oder Kennzeichen bezieht.

Ueble Nachrede ist die Verbreitung einer herabwuerdigenden Behauptung, die nicht nachweislich wahr ist. Entscheidend ist, dass die verfassende Person sich nicht bewusst ist, eine Unwahrheit zu verbreiten. Eine wahre Tatsachenbehauptung ist keine ueble Nachrede.

Auch das Gutheiszen oder Belohnen einer Straftat ist strafbar, ebenso das Gutheiszen einer noch nicht begangenen Tat. Formulierungen wie Person X gehoert an die Wand gestellt koennen strafbar sein, auch wenn keine eigene Drohung ausgesprochen wird.

Sachliche Kritik an einer Religion, einer Weltanschauung oder an Institutionen ist nicht strafbar, auch wenn sie scharf formuliert ist. Strafbar wird sie erst, wenn sie in Beschimpfung uebergeht und geeignet ist, den oeffentlichen Frieden zu stoeren.
